questions.q: To find duplicates, you compare every item with every item after it. How many comparisons is that for a list of 10 items?
questions.explain: Item 1 is compared with 9 others, item 2 with 8, and so on down to 1: 9 + 8 + … + 1 = 45, which is 10 × 9 / 2. The formula n × (n − 1) / 2 comes from counting pairs.

questions.q: The "compare every pair" approach takes 1 second on a list of 5,000 payments. Roughly how long on 50,000 payments?
questions.explain: The number of pairs grows with the square of the list. Ten times more items means about a hundred times more comparisons. That is why you count the steps of an idea before trusting it on real data.

questions.q: Why is the Set version of duplicate detection so much faster than the nested loops?
questions.explain: The Set remembers every value seen so far and answers has instantly. So the work is one step per item instead of one step per pair. The price is the extra memory for the Set.
options: It looks at each item once and asks the Set "have I seen this?", which is one quick step
Sets can only hold strings, which are faster
It stops at the first duplicate

questions.q: The duplicate finder keeps a second Set called reported. What would happen without it, for ["PAY-7", "PAY-7", "PAY-7"]?
questions.explain: The second and third copies are both "already seen", so each would be added to the result. The requirement was to report each duplicated reference once, so the function remembers what it has already reported.
options: PAY-7 would be reported twice, once for each extra copy
PAY-7 would not be reported at all

questions.q: A counting function does counts[product] = counts[product] + 1; without starting new products at 0. What do the counts become?
questions.explain: A key that was never stored reads as undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN. Every later + 1 keeps it NaN. Start unseen keys at a known value first.
options: Correct, because JavaScript starts at 0 automatically
1 for every product, however many were sold
An error that stops the program

questions.q: Bread and Milk both sold 12, and nothing sold more. Why does bestSellers return both instead of just the first one it found?
questions.explain: Which tied product comes "first" depends only on the order of the data, not on anything the manager cares about. Ties are an edge case to decide on purpose; here the decision is "report them all".
options: Because objects cannot return a single value
Picking one would hide an equally good product; returning all ties is the honest answer
Because the loop cannot stop early

questions.q: A support agent searches for an email that no customer has. What should the search function do?
questions.explain: Not finding something is an expected outcome, not a failure of the program. null means "deliberately nothing" and the caller decides what to show.
options: Throw an error, because the input was wrong
Return null, a normal "nothing found" answer the caller can show as a message

questions.q: The same list of 20,000 customers is searched by email 10,000 times a day. What is the better plan?
questions.explain: Building the table costs one walk through the list. After that each search is one step instead of up to 20,000. This table is called an index, and databases use exactly this idea.
options: Walk the list for every search, starting from the end
Build a lookup table from email to customer once, then answer each search with one lookup
Sort the list after every search

questions.q: Dates are stored as text and compared with <. Which format compares correctly?
questions.explain: Text compares character by character from the left. It matches date order only when the biggest unit comes first and every part has a fixed width: four-digit year, two-digit month, two-digit day (the ISO 8601 form).

questions.q: Why does the order filter build a new list instead of removing unwanted orders from the original?
questions.explain: A function that changes its input has a side effect every caller must know about. Returning a new list leaves the original as it was, which is what the "original untouched" test checks.
options: Removing items from a list is not possible in JavaScript
Other code still uses the original orders, and quietly changing them would break it
Because the filter must run twice

questions.q: The board function creates { todo: [], doing: [], done: [], other: [] } before looking at any task. Why?
questions.explain: Grouping only by the statuses that appear would make the Doing column vanish on a day without Doing tasks. Creating the known groups first is a decision about the output shape.
options: JavaScript requires every key to exist before a loop
So a column with no tasks today still exists and the screen always shows all columns
So the tasks are sorted by status

questions.q: A task arrives with status "blocked", which the board does not know. What does the workshop do with it, and why?
questions.explain: A task that silently disappears is worse than an odd-looking column. Keeping it visible, with its real status, lets someone notice and fix the data.
options: Drops it, because it does not fit any column
Puts it in To do, the first column
Puts it in an other group with its status, so nothing disappears silently
Stops the program with an error

questions.q: Pages are numbered from 1 and hold 20 products each. At which list position does page 3 start?
questions.explain: Page p starts at (p − 1) × size: (3 − 1) × 20 = 40. Positions 40 to 59 are the 41st to 60th products.

questions.q: There are 41 products and 20 per page. How many pages are there?
questions.explain: 41 / 20 is 2.05, and the one leftover product still needs a page, so round up with Math.ceil: 3 pages, the last holding one product.

questions.q: Someone asks for page 5 when there are only 4 pages. Why does the workshop return an empty page instead of "invalid"?
questions.explain: Page 0 or −1 is always a caller mistake, but a page just past the end can come from normal use. An empty page plus the real total lets the website say "no more products".
options: It can happen honestly, for example when products were deleted while someone was browsing
Because page numbers are never checked
Because 5 is not a whole number

questions.q: Sales are 900, 700, 700 and 500. With competition ranking (ties share a rank, the next rank skips), what are the ranks?
questions.explain: The two 700s share rank 2. The agent with 500 has three people ahead of them, so they are 4th. (1, 2, 2, 3 is another valid scheme, but it has to be a decision you test.)

questions.q: Why does the leaderboard sort tied agents by name?
questions.explain: Tied agents still share a rank. The second rule only fixes the order in which they are listed, so it does not change between runs or look unfair.
options: Because names are more important than sales
So tied agents appear in the same, predictable order every week
Because sorting by numbers alone is not allowed
To give the alphabetically first agent the better rank

questions.q: The leaderboard uses agents.toSorted(compare) instead of agents.sort(compare). What is the difference that matters here?
questions.explain: The list of agents belongs to the caller. Rearranging it in place is a side effect that can break other code relying on its order; the test team[0].name checks it was left alone.
options: toSorted returns a sorted copy; sort rearranges the caller's own list

questions.q: The warehouse has 5 bags of rice. Movements: "sell 8", then "receive 10". What is the stock at the end of the day?
questions.explain: Movements are applied in the order they happened. At the time of the sale there were only 5 bags, so it is rejected; the delivery then brings the stock to 15. The reverse order would give 7.
options: 15, because the sale is rejected when it happens (only 5 in stock)

questions.q: Why does endOfDay put impossible movements on a rejected list with a reason, instead of just skipping them?
questions.explain: Silently skipping hides the problem; letting stock go negative corrupts the totals. Rejecting with a reason keeps the numbers right and the problem visible.
options: Because JavaScript cannot skip items in a loop
A skipped movement is a real problem (theft, a typo, a missing delivery) that a person needs to see and investigate
To make the stock numbers larger
Because the test requires a list

questions.q: The check helper in this workshop compares JSON.stringify(actual) with JSON.stringify(expected). Why not just actual === expected?
questions.explain: ["A"] === ["A"] is false: === on lists asks "is this the same list?", not "do they look the same?". The JSON text of both is ["A"], so comparing text compares contents, including order.
options: Two separate lists or objects are never ===, even with the same contents; comparing their JSON text compares the contents

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first time a product appears, counts[product] is undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN. After that, NaN + 1 is still NaN.

questions.q: This duplicate finder has no reported set. What does it print?
questions.explain: Every copy after the first is reported: the second and third A, then the second B. To report each duplicated value once, also remember what was already reported.

questions.q: This pagination uses page * size as the start. What does it print?
questions.explain: Pages count from 1 but positions from 0, so page 1 must start at (1 − 1) × 3 = 0. With n * size the first page skips items 1 to 3 completely: an off-by-one error of a whole page.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: slice(start, end) stops before end and never runs past the list, so a partial page just has fewer items and a page past the end is empty. 5 items at 2 per page is 2.5, rounded up to 3 pages.

questions.q: This ranking code sets rank = rank + 1 for each new score. What does it print?
questions.explain: This is "dense ranking": ties share a rank and the next rank does not skip. The workshop's leaderboard uses rank = i + 1 instead, which skips to 4. Both are valid; the choice must be deliberate and tested.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With the fixed YYYY-MM-DD form, text order equals date order. In "2026-9-30" the sixth character is "9", which comes after "1" in "2026-10-01", so the comparison is wrong. Equal texts pass >=, which is how an inclusive boundary works.

questions.q: Two records share an email by mistake. What does this print?
questions.explain: return ends the function at the first match, so record 3 is never looked at. A missing email falls through to return null. The duplicate email is a data problem that the duplicate finder from problem 1 would catch.

questions.q: This grouping creates columns only for statuses it sees. What does it print?
questions.explain: No task had the status "doing", so that key was never created and reading it gives undefined. A screen that expects three columns would break. Create the known groups first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 5 − 3 = 2; selling 4 with only 2 is rejected; + 6 = 8; − 4 = 4. const [type, qty] of movements unpacks each little two-item list into two variables, which the JavaScript course calls destructuring.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.ceil rounds up: 2.25 becomes 3, an exact 2 stays 2, and 0 stays 0 (an empty list has no pages). Math.floor rounds down, which would lose the partial last page.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Milk starts the list with 3. Bread beats it, so the list becomes just Bread. Eggs ties with 5 and is added. A new best replaces the list; a tie extends it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toSorted returns a new sorted list and leaves sales alone. sort rearranges sales itself. b - a puts larger numbers first; a - b puts smaller numbers first.

questions.q: Write unique(list) that returns a new list with each value only once, keeping the order in which values first appear. Use a Set to remember what you have seen.
questions.explain: One pass, one Set lookup per item. The result list keeps the first-appearance order; an empty input gives an empty output.

questions.q: Count orders by status. Write countByStatus(orders) that returns a lookup table such as { paid: 2, pending: 1 }.
questions.explain: The "count into a table" pattern: start each new key at 0, then add 1. No orders gives an empty table, not an error.

questions.q: Write findBooking(bookings, code) that returns the booking whose code matches, ignoring case and spaces at the ends of the searched code, or null if there is none.
questions.explain: Clean the input once, walk the list, and return at the first match. "Not found" returns null. ?.guest reads guest only if there is a booking, which the JavaScript course explains.

questions.q: Write pageOf(items, page, size) that returns the items for a 1-based page number, or "invalid" when page or size is below 1.
questions.explain: Page p starts at (p − 1) × size. slice handles the partial last page and a page past the end without extra code; only impossible page numbers are refused.

questions.q: Group orders by customer: write ordersByCustomer(orders) that returns a table from customer name to a list of order ids, in input order.
questions.explain: Grouping is counting with lists instead of numbers: start each new key with an empty list, then push. Walking the input in order keeps each group in order.

questions.q: An inventory lists products with a price in kobo and a quantity. Write stockValue(products) that returns the total value in kobo, and "invalid" if any quantity is negative.
questions.explain: 1,000,000 + 999,000 = 1,999,000 kobo. An empty inventory is worth 0. A negative quantity would lower the value, so it is refused as soon as it is seen.

questions.q: Write topScorers(students) that returns the names of every student with the highest score (ties included), in input order. An empty class returns an empty list.
questions.explain: Starting best at null (not 0) means a class whose best score is 0 still has a top scorer. A new best replaces the list; a tie extends it.

questions.q: Write overdue(tasks, today) that returns the titles of tasks that are not done and whose due date (text in YYYY-MM-DD form) is before today. A task due today is not overdue.
questions.explain: "Before today" is <, so the task due today is left out. Fixed-width dates compare correctly as text. Today is an input, so the result never changes by itself.
